articles.title: Improving social media for democratic discourse
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.10816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social media have expanded opportunities for communication and political participation, but today's dominant platforms are optimized primarily for engagement and advertising revenue, contributing to concerns about polarization, misinformation, social isolation, and loss of civility. We explore how social media might instead be deliberately designed to support democratic discourse, collective deliberation, and collective intelligence. articles.title: Political polarization and mental wellbeing: asymmetric evidence for bidirectionality
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.11601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A growing body of evidence suggests that political polarization and mental health and wellbeing influence each other. Yet the two directions, how polarization shapes mental wellbeing and how mental wellbeing shapes polarization, remain siloed across disciplines. We review both literatures to evaluate the strength and alignment of evidence for bidirectional effects. articles.title: Auditing AI-Washing in German Startups: A Mixed-Methods Study of Marketing Claims and Perceptions
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.11788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-washing is the use of 'AI' as a marketing term where products' claims are exaggerated, likely to capture the hype from investors and consumers. In this paper, we examine how startups market AI and how people perceive those claims. We audited the German startup market, applying an annotation codebook of seven dimensions to 100 startups and conducting 63 expert interviews. articles.title: Automated Disinformation and Malicious AI Swarms: Risks for Democracy and Development in Africa
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.11930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is reshaping how information is produced, accessed, and circulated, while enabling disinformation campaigns of increasing scale and sophistication. There is currently no clear evidence that fully autonomous AI swarms conduct influence operations at scale, but their enabling capabilities are advancing. articles.summary: arXiv:2610.12125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is assumed that a natural way to improve the pedagogical quality of large language model tutors is to define a metric of instructional performance and fine-tune the model against it. articles.title: Execution and Evaluation: A New Occupational Measure and Long-Run Employment Gradients
articles.summary: arXiv:2607.20807v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence automates execution more readily than evaluation: producing output is cheap, judging whether it is correct is not. Exposure measures rank tasks by whether AI can perform them, not by which function the human supplies. I score all $19{,}265$ O*NET task statements under fixed rubrics to build occupation-level execution and AI-capability shares. articles.title: Maintaining Human Verification Capacity under Automation
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.38459v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Human verification depends on expertise that must be maintained before it is needed. This paper links reliance on automated checks, investment in human checking ability, and performance during an interruption. Better checking lowers the error reduction gained from an extra unit of human skill while the checker works. articles.summary: arXiv:2610.10914v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decisions that will shape future fusion facilities, including the production of waste, the management of tritium, the achievement of safety, and impacts on land, water, and local communities, are increasingly becoming sociotechnical in nature. articles.title: Risk Ceilings and Development Deadlines: Pacing AI under Uncertain Safety Productivity
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.11093v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a regulator promise both a risk ceiling and a development deadline when safety productivity is unknown? articles.title: Can a System-One LLM Perform Knowledge Tracing When Few or No Learners Are Logged?
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.11135v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) models need many logged learners, so a new course or platform starts without a usable model. In LLM-based KT the LLM generates the answer, which we call System-Two; it is either fine-tuned on the target data or reasons and votes over ten samples, which is slow and gives coarse probabilities.
